rubric.why: Award for explaining how the user communicates with the computer.

items.followUp: How can you compare two algorithms to decide which one is more efficient?

rubric.why: An efficient algorithm must still solve the problem correctly.
rubric.how: First ensure each algorithm produces the correct result.

rubric.why: Time taken is a key measure of efficiency.
rubric.how: Compare how long each algorithm takes, including for larger inputs.

rubric.why: Memory use is another key measure of efficiency.
rubric.how: Compare the amount of memory each algorithm needs.

rubric.why: Award for applying the comparison to select an algorithm.
rubric.description: Selects the algorithm using the comparison.
rubric.how: Choose the correct algorithm that uses less time and memory for the problem.

modelAnswer: Check that each algorithm gives the correct result.
Compare their execution time, especially as the input size increases.
Compare the memory each algorithm requires.
Choose the correct algorithm that uses fewer resources overall.

items.followUp: Explain bus and ring network topologies.

rubric.why: The central connecting device is the defining feature of star topology.
rubric.description: Identifies the central device in a star.
rubric.how: State that all computers connect to a central hub or switch.

rubric.why: Award for explaining how devices are connected in a star.
rubric.how: Explain that each computer has a separate connection to the central device.

rubric.why: A mesh connects devices to one another rather than relying on a single central device.
rubric.how: State that each device is connected to every other device in a full mesh.

rubric.why: Award for a valid feature or comparison of mesh topology.
rubric.description: Gives a mesh feature or its cost implication.
rubric.how: Mention that mesh is reliable because alternate links can remain available, but it requires many links and is costly.

modelAnswer: In a star topology, every computer has a separate connection to a central hub or switch.
If the central device fails, communication across the star network is disrupted.
In a full mesh topology, each device is connected to every other device.
Mesh is reliable because other links may still work if one link fails, but it requires many connections and is expensive.

items.followUp: Define cyber-crime and explain three examples.

rubric.why: Award for defining cyber-crime as an illegal activity involving computers or digital technology.
rubric.how: Explain that cyber-crime is an illegal activity carried out using computers, networks, or the Internet.

rubric.why: Award for naming and explaining one type.
rubric.how: Describe hacking as gaining unauthorised access to a computer or network.

rubric.why: Award for naming and explaining another type.
rubric.description: Explains phishing or a comparable type.
rubric.how: Describe phishing as using deceptive messages or websites to steal personal information.

rubric.why: Award for naming and explaining a third valid type.
rubric.description: Explains a third type of cyber-crime.
rubric.how: Give another type, such as identity theft, cyberbullying, or online fraud, with a brief explanation.

modelAnswer: Cyber-crime is an illegal activity carried out using computers, networks, or the Internet.
Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer or network.
Phishing uses deceptive messages or websites to steal personal information.
Identity theft is the misuse of another person's personal information to impersonate them.

items.followUp: Write two advantages of an algorithm.

rubric.why: Award for one valid disadvantage, such as the time needed to write an algorithm.
rubric.how: State a valid drawback, for example that writing an algorithm can be time-consuming.

rubric.why: Award for a second distinct disadvantage.
rubric.how: State another valid drawback, such as difficulty understanding a complex or lengthy algorithm.

modelAnswer: Writing an algorithm for a complex problem can be time-consuming.
A lengthy or complex algorithm can be difficult to understand.

items.followUp: What is an unordered list in HTML, and which tag is used to create it?

rubric.why: Award for identifying an ordered list as a list of items.
rubric.description: Identifies it as a list of items.
rubric.how: State that an ordered list is a list containing items.

rubric.why: Award for explaining that items are numbered or for naming the HTML tag.
rubric.description: Describes its ordered appearance or gives its tag.
rubric.how: Explain that items appear in sequence, usually numbered, and/or name the <ol> tag.

modelAnswer: An ordered list is a list of items displayed in a particular sequence, usually with numbers.
In HTML, it is created using the <ol> tag, with each item placed in an <li> element.
